question: Why is an evaluation you cannot reproduce described as worse than none?
options: It produces numbers that drift between runs and lead you to false conclusions
It always takes longer to run than the training run it is meant to measure
It prevents the model from being checkpointed until the evaluation finishes cleanly
It forces you to retrain the tokenizer between experiments so the vocabularies match
explanation: Research velocity is bounded by how quickly and reliably you can measure. A non-reproducible evaluation gives drifting numbers, so differences between experiments may be noise and you draw wrong conclusions. That is worse than having no number at all.

question: What is the ML-project equivalent of a software project's test suite, according to the 'evaluation as a first-class discipline' view?
options: The training loop's gradient-clipping logic, which guards every update against bad batches and silent divergence
The data loader's shuffling routine, which guarantees every experiment sees the same examples in the same order
The checkpoint-saving code, which records every model state so that any experiment can be restored and rerun
The evaluation harness: the code that, given a model, produces the metrics decisions are made on
explanation: Just as you would not ship code without tests, you should not make ML decisions without a harness that measures the model. It deserves production-code seriousness: documented interfaces, deterministic behavior, and its own tests.

question: What does the evaluation harness return so its results can be logged, compared, and asserted on?
options: GPU tensors with autograd graphs
Raw logits for every scored token
Plain Python floats and indices
Matplotlib figures of the loss curve
explanation: The harness orchestrates the forward pass and log_softmax over held-out data and returns plain floats (perplexity, log-likelihoods) and integer indices (chosen options). These are easy to log and assert on, unlike tensors carrying graphs.

question: Which three properties make an evaluation harness trustworthy?
options: Fast (one pass per eval set), GPU-only (every metric computed on device), and distributed (sharded across ranks so results match)
Deterministic (same inputs give the same numbers), documented (shapes/dtype/device stated), and tested (metrics checked against known answers)
Stochastic (fresh samples each run to avoid overfitting), cached (results reused across runs), and approximate (subsampled eval sets)
Fine-tuned (the model adapted to each benchmark), calibrated (temperature-scaled logits), and decontaminated (overlaps removed first)
explanation: A harness must be deterministic, documented, and tested; lose any one and its numbers become unreliable. Speed and hardware are conveniences, not trustworthiness properties.

question: What are the inputs to evaluate_perplexity in the llmre harness?
options: A list of raw held-out strings, a tokenizer to encode them, a learning rate, and a number of evaluation epochs
A flat 1-D torch.long tensor of held-out token ids, a block_size, a batch_size, and an optional max_batches
A 2-D float tensor of precomputed logits of shape (N, V), a target tensor of shape (N,), and a temperature
A model checkpoint path, a vocabulary file, a block_size, and the device on which to load the weights to
explanation: evaluate_perplexity takes the model, a flat long tensor data of held-out ids, the context length block_size, batch_size, and an optional max_batches to stop early on huge streams. Tokenization happens before.

question: How does evaluate_perplexity form input and target for window i of length T?
options: x = data[i·T : i·T + T] and y = data[i·T + 1 : i·T + 1 + T], the same window shifted one token right
x = data[i·T : i·T + T] and y = data[i·T : i·T + T], the same window used as both input and target
x = data[i : i + T] and y = data[i + T], a sliding window that predicts one single next token per step
x and y are random overlapping windows of length T sampled fresh for each batch, as in the training loader
explanation: Non-overlapping windows are cut from the stream, and the target is the input shifted by one, the standard next-token setup. Using the same slice for y is a bug that makes the task trivial.

question: Why does evaluate_perplexity cut the stream into non-overlapping windows of length block_size?
options: Because overlapping windows would require gradient computation across windows, which no_grad forbids during evaluation
Because the model cannot accept sequences shorter than its vocabulary size, so every window must be exactly block_size
Because non-overlapping windows always give the lowest possible perplexity, which is the number papers conventionally report
So each held-out target token is scored once with a fixed context length, making the metric well-defined and reproducible
explanation: Non-overlapping windows partition the stream so each target token is counted once under a defined block_size. Overlap would double-count tokens; gradients are irrelevant here. Lower perplexity is not the goal — consistency is.

question: How does evaluate_perplexity aggregate per-batch losses?
options: Average the per-batch mean losses directly, giving each batch equal weight whatever its size, then exponentiate the result
Take the minimum batch loss across all batches as the most reliable estimate, then exponentiate it to get perplexity
Token-weighted: multiply each batch's mean loss by its token count, sum, and divide by total tokens, then exponentiate
Exponentiate each batch's mean loss into a perplexity first, then average the per-batch perplexities weighted by token count
explanation: Accumulating float(loss) * n_tok and dividing by total_tokens gives exactly the mean over all target tokens, independent of how windows divide into batches. Averaging batch means over-weights a small final batch; averaging per-batch perplexities is also not the same as exp of the mean loss.

question: Why does evaluation run under torch.no_grad() with the model in eval() mode?
options: no_grad enables dropout for regularization during scoring; eval() turns on gradient checkpointing to save activation memory
no_grad converts the weights to fp16 so evaluation runs faster; eval() freezes the tokenizer so token ids cannot change
no_grad builds no autograd graph, saving memory and time; eval() disables dropout so the numbers are deterministic
Both are required for the loss to be computed in nats rather than bits, since training mode uses a base-2 cross-entropy
explanation: torch.no_grad() stops recording operations for backprop, so no graph or saved activations are retained. model.eval() switches dropout (and batch-norm, if present) to inference behavior so an input always yields the same logits. Neither changes units or precision.

question: What does model.eval() change for a GPT with dropout?
options: It stops gradients from being computed for every forward pass
It disables dropout so a given input always produces the same logits
It freezes the weights so that the optimizer can no longer change any of them
It switches the model to half precision for faster inference
explanation: eval() flips modules like dropout and batch-norm into inference behavior; for the GPT it disables dropout, giving deterministic outputs. Gradient tracking is controlled by no_grad, not eval(), and eval() does not touch precision or the optimizer.

question: Which statement correctly describes the separate roles of model.eval() and torch.no_grad() in evaluation?
options: eval() is required for determinism and no_grad() for memory; forgetting either does not change the correctness of a single deterministic pass
eval() is required for memory and no_grad() for determinism; forgetting either changes the value that a single deterministic pass computes
Both are required for correctness, because without them the cross-entropy is computed on dropped-out logits and so the loss value itself is wrong
Only one is needed, because eval() automatically disables gradient tracking, so wrapping evaluation in no_grad() as well is redundant
explanation: eval() removes dropout randomness; no_grad() avoids retaining the graph. Neither changes the mathematical value of one deterministic pass. eval() does not disable gradient tracking, so both are needed.

question: In evaluate_perplexity, how is the number of windows computed from a stream of data.numel() tokens?
options: data.numel() // block_size, using every token as an input, with the very last target wrapping around
data.numel() - block_size, giving one overlapping window per possible starting position
(data.numel() + 1) // block_size, rounding up so the final partial window is included
(data.numel() - 1) // block_size, since each window needs one extra token for the shifted target
explanation: Each window needs block_size inputs plus one more token for the last target, so the last token can only be a target; hence (numel − 1) // block_size non-overlapping windows. One window per start position would mean overlapping windows.

question: In evaluate_perplexity, why would averaging per-batch losses directly give a wrong answer?
options: It under-weights the first batch, whose loss is inflated by warmup, so the mean comes out too low
It double-counts tokens that appear in several overlapping windows, inflating their weight in the overall average
It converts nats to bits incorrectly, because a mean of per-batch means is taken in base 2 instead of base e
It over-weights a small final batch, whereas token weighting reproduces the single mean over all target tokens
explanation: Each batch loss is already a mean over its tokens, so a mean of means gives every batch equal weight regardless of size. Weighting by token count makes the result independent of batching.

question: What does sequence_loglikelihood(model, ids) compute?
options: The perplexity of the sequence averaged over sliding windows of block_size tokens with stride 1
The probability of the sequence's first token only, given a beginning-of-sequence token in front
The total log-probability Σ_t ln q(x_t | x_<t) over the sequence, from a single forward pass
The entropy of the model's next-token distribution at the last position, from a single forward pass
explanation: It sums the conditional log-probabilities of tokens 1 … L−1 given their prefixes. One forward pass suffices because the logits at position t are the model's prediction for token t+1.

question: In sequence_loglikelihood, why are logits[:-1] paired with ids[1:]?
options: The first logit is always padding from the beginning-of-sequence slot, so it must be dropped before pairing with the targets
The last position would predict a token past the end, and ids[1:] are exactly the tokens predicted by positions 0 … L−2
ids[1:] removes the end-of-sequence token, which the model never has to predict, and logits[:-1] drops its matching row
It reverses the sequence so that the model reads right to left, which is how causal attention lines up logits with targets
explanation: Logits at position p predict token p+1, so dropping the final position and the first target aligns predictions with what they predict. This index arithmetic is the whole trick.

question: Why is the first token of a sequence never scored by sequence_loglikelihood under a plain LM?
options: It has no prefix, so there is no conditional ln q(x_0 | x_<0) to score
The first token is always a special BOS token with probability 1
Scoring it would require a second forward pass with a dummy prefix token
The first logit is discarded for numerical stability inside log_softmax
explanation: The score of each token is its probability given preceding tokens; the first token has none. The code enforces this by predicting tokens 1 … L−1 from positions 0 … L−2.

question: What does the value returned by sequence_loglikelihood mean?
options: A single Python float ≤ 0; less negative means the model finds the sequence more probable
A positive Python float where larger values mean the model finds the sequence less probable
A tensor of shape (L, V) holding the model's log-probabilities at every position
A perplexity value ≥ 1, the exponential of the mean negative log-likelihood per token
explanation: It returns float(chosen.sum()), the sum of log-probabilities, which is at most 0. A value closer to 0 means higher probability. It is not perplexity and is not a tensor.

question: In sequence_loglikelihood with ids of shape (L,), what are the shapes of logits after taking batch element 0, of logp, and of chosen?
options: logits (1, L); logp (L, V); chosen (L,)
logits (V, L); logp (V, L−1); chosen (V, L−1)
logits (L, V); logp (L, V); chosen (1,)
logits (L, V); logp (L−1, V); chosen (L−1,)
explanation: The model returns (1, L, V); indexing [0] gives (L, V). log_softmax(logits[:-1]) is (L−1, V), and gathering the target token per row gives chosen of shape (L−1,), which is then summed.

question: Where do the option tokens sit in [context; option], and which logits predict them, in multiple_choice_score?
options: At positions 0 … L_o − 1, at the front of the sequence, predicted by logits at those same positions 0 … L_o − 1
At positions L_c + 1 … L_c + L_o, after a separator token, predicted by logits at positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1
At absolute positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1, predicted by logits at positions L_c − 1 … L_c + L_o − 2
At absolute positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1, predicted by logits at those same positions L_c … L_c + L_o − 1
explanation: Option tokens follow the L_c context tokens, and since logits at p predict token p+1, they are predicted by positions one earlier. This is the §3 index arithmetic offset by the context length.

question: How does multiple_choice_score handle zero-shot versus few-shot evaluation?
options: It requires a separate few_shot flag that enables a second forward pass over the demonstrations
Identically; the number of in-context examples only changes how many tokens are in context_ids
It scores the demonstrations as additional options in few-shot mode and drops them from the argmax
It only supports zero-shot scoring; few-shot evaluation needs a model fine-tuned on the examples
explanation: Because it accepts any model(seq) -> (logits, loss) and any context, demonstrations are simply more context tokens. The scoring logic does not change.

section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
question: Why must every source of randomness be seeded before an evaluation that uses any?
options: Perplexity computed in eval() mode changes from run to run unless the global seed is fixed before each run
Anything involving sampling, such as generating completions for pass@k, is only reproducible if seeded
Seeds control the learning rate and warmup schedule used during evaluation, so unseeded runs differ
Seeding is needed to make torch.no_grad() take effect, since the graph is otherwise built at random
explanation: Perplexity and log-likelihood scoring are deterministic in eval() mode, but sampling-based evaluation is not; seeding torch, NumPy, and Python makes it reproducible. Seeds do not affect no_grad or learning rates.

section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
question: Why must the held-out stream and benchmark question set be frozen and versioned?
options: Comparing run B with run A is only valid if both were measured on the same data; changing the eval set silently turns comparison into noise
Because the model memorizes whatever eval set it is shown, so any change to the set leaks new answers into the weights over successive runs
Because unfrozen eval sets cannot be tokenized consistently, since the BPE merges are refit from scratch whenever the underlying text changes
Because versioned data is stored contiguously on disk and runs faster on GPUs, which keeps evaluation cheap enough to run after every step
explanation: A comparison between experiments is meaningful only on identical evaluation data. Altering the data changes the numbers for reasons unrelated to the models.

section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
question: Which items belong in a versioned evaluation config stored next to each result?
options: Only the final metric value and the date it was computed, since the code in the repository at that date fully determines everything else
Only the model's parameter count, the GPU type, and the driver version, since the hardware is what makes evaluation numbers drift
Only the random seed used for the run, since with the seed fixed every other part of the evaluation is fully deterministic and needs no record
Checkpoint hash, tokenizer version, block_size, batch_size, eval-set version/hash, scoring rule, few-shot count, and library versions
explanation: Everything that can affect the number must be recorded so it can be regenerated months later: checkpoint, tokenizer, block/batch sizes, eval-set version, scoring rule (summed vs normalized), shot count, and library versions.

section: 5. Reproducibility: seeds, fixed eval set, versioned config
question: What is the most common silent reproducibility bug in evaluation?
options: Running evaluation on CPU instead of GPU, so fused kernels change the low-order bits and every reported metric shifts slightly between machines
Logging metrics as floats instead of strings, so rounding in the experiment tracker silently changes the third decimal place of every logged metric
Comparing two numbers produced under different settings, e.g. another block_size, normalization, decontaminated vs raw eval set, or tokenizer
Evaluating more often than once per epoch, so the held-out set is seen many times and slowly leaks into the model through checkpoint selection
explanation: Numbers computed under different settings look comparable but are not. Logging the full config with every metric makes such mismatches visible. Hardware choice does not change a deterministic metric meaningfully.

section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
question: What is an evaluation regression test?
options: A linear regression fit of validation loss against training steps, used to predict when the metric will stop improving
A test that reruns a short training job from a fixed seed and checks that the training loss still decreases as it did before the change
A test that pins a metric to a known value or known-answer synthetic case, so a refactor that changes the number fails loudly
A benchmark run comparing the current model against the previous model release, failing if the new score is any lower
explanation: Like regression tests in software, it catches changes that quietly break behavior: if a refactor shifts the metric on a known-answer case, the test fails before the wrong number reaches an experiment.

section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
question: What does the uniform-model regression test assert about evaluate_perplexity?
options: A model returning all-zero logits over V tokens must give a held-out perplexity of exactly 1
A model returning all-zero logits over V tokens must give held-out perplexity exactly V
A uniform model over V tokens must give held-out perplexity ln V, the uniform cross-entropy
A uniform model must give perplexity 0, because all-zero logits carry no signal about the data
explanation: All-zero logits produce a uniform softmax with probability 1/V per token, so cross-entropy is ln V and perplexity exp(ln V) = V. evaluate_perplexity(UniformModel(V), data, block_size=16) must return V.

section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
question: How do the constructed-logits tests pin the behavior of multiple_choice_score?
options: A model putting a large logit on one token must make the scorer pick the option built from that token, and swapping options must flip the answer
A model with random logits must make the scorer pick option 0 more than half the time, and adding a third option must not change the winner
A model with all-zero logits must make the scorer pick the longest option, and turning on length normalization must make it pick the shortest one instead
The scorer must return the same answer index regardless of option order, and a model with constant logits must always pick the first option
explanation: By constructing a model whose preference is known, the test asserts the scorer picks the favored option and that reordering the options flips the returned index, pinning the scoring logic.

section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
question: What does the length-normalization regression test in test_eval.py check?
options: That length normalization never changes the chosen option when the per-token confidences of the two options are known in advance
That the normalized rule always picks the shortest option, while the summed rule picks whichever option contains the most confident single token
That normalization makes every option's score positive, so the argmax over options is well defined even for very long options
With two known per-token confidences, the summed rule picks the short option and the normalized rule picks the longer, higher-confidence one
explanation: The test reproduces the summed-vs-normalized flip: the sum favors the short option, normalization favors the longer option whose tokens are each more probable. This locks in the normalization behavior.

section: 6. Regression testing: lock the metrics in
question: What makes a good known-answer test for an evaluation harness?
options: Inputs drawn from the real benchmark, with the expected answers recorded from the current harness output so that any later change in the number is caught
Inputs chosen randomly on each run to cover more cases over time, with the expected metric recomputed by the harness on every single run
Inputs that produce the largest possible metric values, e.g. a model that is always confidently wrong, so overflow and edge cases get exercised
Inputs whose correct metric you can compute by hand, e.g. uniform model gives perplexity V, or all-wrong predictions at confidence 0.9 give ECE 0.9
explanation: Known-answer tests compare the harness to values derived independently by hand, so any deviation reveals a bug. Snapshotting the current harness output would lock in existing bugs, and random inputs are not reproducible.

section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
question: In the tiny-GPT harness demonstration, why is the model trained on the repeating stream 0, 1, 2, …, V−1, 0, 1, …?
options: Because it is effectively random noise to the model, so its perplexity should stay at about V however long it trains
Because it exercises the tokenizer's merge rules on a stream whose byte pairs repeat in a known, countable order
Because its next token is fully learnable, so a few dozen steps suffice to drive perplexity well below V
Because it maximizes the number of distinct n-grams in the stream, so the held-out windows never overlap with training
explanation: The pattern is deterministic: every token determines the next. A 2-layer GPT learns it in a few dozen steps, demonstrating the harness on a real model with a predictable outcome.

section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
question: What does the tiny-GPT demonstration show before and after a few dozen training steps?
options: Before, perplexity is about 1 because the model is untrained; after, it rises toward V = 16 as the scorer learns to prefer option 11
Before, perplexity is about V = 16; after, it drops well below V and the scorer prefers the true continuation 5 over 11 after context [0,1,2,3,4]
Before and after, perplexity stays at about V = 16, because the tiny model is too small to learn the pattern in a few dozen steps
After training, perplexity drops well below V, but the scorer prefers option 11 over 5 after context [0,1,2,3,4] because 11 has the higher token id
explanation: An untrained model is near uniform (perplexity ≈ V). After learning the pattern, perplexity falls well below 16, and multiple_choice_score returns 0, choosing token 5 as the continuation of 0,1,2,3,4.

section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
question: Why does the tiny-GPT demonstration call torch.manual_seed(0) and set dropout=0.0?
options: To make initialization and training sampling reproducible and to remove dropout randomness, so the test is deterministic
To speed up training by skipping random initialization of the weights and removing the dropout masks from every forward pass
Because GPTConfig requires a seed of 0 and dropout of 0.0 whenever it is used to build a model on a CPU-only machine
Because dropout must be 0 for perplexity to be finite, and seeding is what makes the uniform-model test hit exactly V
explanation: Fixing the seed makes the random initialization and randomly sampled training windows identical every run; dropout 0 removes stochasticity from the forward pass. Together they make the test reproducible.

section: 7. Running the harness on a tiny trained model
question: What does the full tiny-GPT test assert?
options: That perplexity is finite and positive and that the correct option wins
That held-out perplexity equals exactly 1 after a few dozen training steps
That training loss falls below 0.01 nats and the scorer picks option 0
That the model generates the full pattern from an empty prompt
explanation: Exact post-training perplexity is not pinned; the test asserts it is finite and positive and that multiple_choice_score picks the true continuation. It runs in under a second on CPU.

question: What hardware is needed for the evaluation-harness lesson and its tests?
options: At least one 24 GB GPU, since evaluation keeps the optimizer state and saved activations of the full model in memory
A multi-GPU node, because the token-weighted perplexity requires a distributed all-reduce across at least two ranks
A TPU or TPU emulator, because the harness relies on XLA-specific operations for its log_softmax and gather steps
Any CPU is fully sufficient; a GPU only helps when evaluating a full-size model over millions of held-out tokens
explanation: The harness is inference-only and the toy example finishes in well under a second on CPU. On a real corpus with a full-size model it becomes a batched inference job where a GPU helps. No optimizer state is needed.

question: Why does evaluation under torch.no_grad() use far less GPU memory than a training step?
options: The model weights are automatically quantized to 4 bits inside no_grad
Only the first layer of the model is executed when no autograd graph is recorded
There is no optimizer state and no saved activations for a backward pass
The batch size is forced to 1 and the sequence length to the block size
explanation: Training memory includes optimizer state, gradients, and activations saved for backward. Evaluation under no_grad needs only the weights and the transient activations of the forward pass.

question: A teammate changes evaluate_perplexity to average per-batch losses directly. Batch A has mean 2.0 over 800 tokens and batch B mean 4.0 over 8 tokens. What are the token-weighted and mean-of-means losses?
options: Both equal 3.0, since each batch's mean loss is already token-weighted, so the change is harmless
Token-weighted ≈ 2.02; mean-of-means = 3.0, badly off because the tiny batch gets equal weight
Token-weighted = 3.0; mean-of-means ≈ 2.02, because the mean-of-means favors the large batch
Token-weighted = 4.0; mean-of-means = 2.0, because weighting by tokens favors the higher loss
explanation: Token-weighted: (2.0·800 + 4.0·8)/808 = 1632/808 ≈ 2.02. Mean of means: (2.0 + 4.0)/2 = 3.0. The two agree only when all batches have equal token counts, which fails when the last batch is smaller.

question: What happens if an evaluation runs without model.eval()?
options: Gradients are computed and the optimizer then updates the model's weights after every single evaluation batch
Dropout stays active, so the same input gives different logits each run and the metric is non-deterministic
The loss is reported in bits instead of nats, so the perplexity comes out lower by a factor of ln 2
The model cannot accept target tokens in training mode, so the forward call raises an error at once
explanation: Without eval(), dropout randomly zeroes activations during evaluation, making results vary run to run. It does not update weights — that requires an optimizer step.

question: What happens if an evaluation runs without torch.no_grad()?
options: The values are still correct for one pass, but PyTorch retains the computation graph and evaluation can run out of memory on a real model
The metric becomes non-deterministic, because leaving no_grad off keeps dropout enabled and PyTorch samples new masks each pass
The model's weights are updated during evaluation, because autograd applies the stored gradients to the parameters at the end of every forward
The loss becomes negative, because the retained graph adds the gradient of each token's log-probability back into the value
explanation: Without no_grad, autograd records operations and keeps activations for a backward pass that never comes, inflating memory. Dropout is controlled by eval(), not no_grad.

question: Why is the lack of a regression test on the evaluation harness a common mistake?
options: Without tests the harness runs slower, because results are never cached
Regression tests are required to compute perplexity in the first place
Without tests the harness cannot load checkpoints from older versions
A refactor can silently change the number and you keep trusting it
explanation: Without pinned known-answer tests, a code change that alters a metric goes unnoticed, and wrong numbers flow into experiments. Tests do not affect speed or functionality.

question: An evaluate_perplexity variant returns a far-too-low perplexity. Its targets are ys = data[i*block_size : i*block_size + block_size], the same slice as the inputs. What is wrong?
options: The inputs should be shifted left by one instead of the targets, so the model sees future tokens and predicts the past ones
The block_size is too small for the model, so most positions have almost no context and the loss is clipped toward zero
The targets are not shifted by one, so each position is asked to predict its own input token, making the task trivial
The model is in eval() mode, which turns off dropout and makes held-out loss artificially lower than the true training loss
explanation: Targets must be data[i*block_size + 1 : i*block_size + 1 + block_size]. With unshifted targets the model can read the answer directly, so loss goes near zero and perplexity far too low. eval() mode does not lower loss artificially.

question: Besides the unshifted targets, what smaller second bug is in that faulty evaluate_perplexity variant that appends float(loss) to a list and returns exp(sum(losses)/len(losses))?
options: It exponentiates in base 2 instead of base e, so the perplexity is reported in bits per token
It forgets to call model.eval(), so dropout makes every batch's loss slightly too low on average
The mean of per-batch means is not token-weighted, so a smaller final batch is over-weighted
It omits the torch.no_grad() decorator, so the retained graph adds memory and lowers the loss value
explanation: Averaging batch means gives each batch equal weight regardless of its token count, biasing the result whenever batches are unequal. The variant does call model.eval() and is decorated with torch.no_grad().

question: What is the combined effect of omitting torch.no_grad() and model.eval() from an evaluation harness?
options: Omitting either makes every reported number mathematically wrong, since dropout and the retained graph both change the cross-entropy that is computed
Omitting no_grad risks out-of-memory; omitting eval leaves dropout on and the metric non-deterministic; neither changes one deterministic pass
Omitting no_grad makes results non-deterministic because autograd reorders reductions; omitting eval causes out-of-memory from dropout masks
Neither matters for language models, because GPT-style transformers have no dropout or batch-norm layers and never build a graph at eval time
explanation: no_grad is about memory, eval about determinism. Both are needed for a correct, reproducible, memory-efficient harness, though neither changes the value of one deterministic forward pass. GPTs typically do have dropout.

question: Why is the uniform-model perplexity test a good known-answer case?
options: Its correct value is derivable by hand — cross-entropy ln V, perplexity V — independent of the data or the harness's batching
Because uniform models are what production systems deploy as a safe fallback, so the test mirrors real serving conditions closely
Because it produces the lowest possible perplexity, so any harness bug can only show up as a higher, failing number
Because it requires a trained model, so the same test also checks that the training loop converges to the uniform answer on held-out data
explanation: A uniform distribution gives exactly ln V nats per token on any data, so perplexity must be V regardless of batching. Any deviation exposes a bug such as a bad shift or wrong aggregation. No training is needed.

question: The same model gives perplexity 18.4 with block_size 512 and 21.7 with block_size 128. Can you conclude the first setting is better?
options: Yes — lower perplexity on the same held-out stream always means the better setting, whatever block_size each run happened to use
Yes — but only if both runs used the same batch_size, since batch size is what changes the token weighting of the mean perplexity
No — perplexity is undefined for block_size above 256, so the 18.4 figure must have come from a truncated or otherwise broken evaluation run
No — a longer block_size gives most positions more context, generally lowering perplexity whatever the quality; the configs are not comparable
explanation: Perplexity depends on how much preceding context each position has; longer windows lower it mechanically. To compare fairly, fix block_size and every other setting, which is why the config is versioned with the metric.
